children: VANCOUVER, BC, Aug. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Equity Insider
News Commentary -

For most of the internet's history, the encryption protecting banking, identity, communications, and state secrets has been treated as a settled problem. That assumption is now expiring. As quantum computing advances toward the point where it could break the public-key cryptography the world currently relies on, governments have stopped treating the transition to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) as a research topic and started treating it as a procurement deadline. Standards bodies have finalized quantum-resistant algorithms, national agencies have set migration timelines, and the question facing thousands of organizations has shifted from whether to migrate to how, and how fast. That shift is turning a once-obscure discipline into one of the more strategically important corners of cybersecurity. Active companies in the space this week include: Quantum Secure Encryption Corp. (
) (OTCQB: QSEGF) (FSE: VN80), Palo Alto Networks, Inc. (
), CrowdStrike Holdings, Inc. (
), International Business Machines Corporation (
), and SEALSQ Corp. (

The hardest part of the migration, industry participants increasingly argue, is not swapping one algorithm for another. It is the logistics: an organization first has to discover where cryptography lives across its applications, devices, certificates, and infrastructure, assess where it is exposed, prioritize the risks, and build a structured roadmap to quantum-safe systems without breaking the trust and continuity its operations depend on. That planning-and-readiness layer, rather than the encryption math itself, is where much of the near-term work sits. More background on the sector is available through Equity Insider.

Nowhere is that readiness challenge more concrete than in the public sector and regulated industries, where data sovereignty, local regulation, and trusted infrastructure all complicate the path. Increasingly, the answer is taking the form of partnerships that pair specialized quantum-readiness technology with established local providers of digital trust. One such partnership was announced this week in Malaysia.
A Post-Quantum Partnership Takes Shape in Malaysia
Quantum Secure Encryption Corp. (

) (OTCQB: QSEGF) (FSE: VN80), a post-quantum cybersecurity company focused on quantum-resilient data protection, identity security, secure storage, and cryptographic migration readiness, recently announced a strategic partnership with Pos Digicert Sdn. Bhd. to help Malaysian organizations assess, understand, and strengthen their readiness for the transition to post-quantum cryptography.
Key points from the company's release include:

The partnership pairs Pos Digicert's longstanding expertise in Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), digital certificates, digital identity, and trusted digital services with QSE's quantum-readiness technology and cryptographic-risk expertise.

QSE's readiness suite, which the company identifies as QPrime, QScope, QSim, and QGuard, is designed to help organizations assess their cryptographic posture, identify areas of exposure, prioritize risks, and develop structured improvement roadmaps.

Pos Digicert is described as Malaysia's first licensed Certification Authority, wholly owned by Pos Malaysia Berhad, bringing established relationships across the public and private sectors and deep local digital-trust infrastructure.

The collaboration is intended to support a locally delivered approach, addressing data sovereignty, regulatory requirements, and trusted infrastructure that matter to government agencies and regulated industries, and to span the full journey from discovery and readiness assessment through risk prioritization, remediation planning, migration preparation, and ongoing monitoring.

"PQC readiness is becoming a shared responsibility between technology, governance and trusted local ecosystems," said Ted Carefoot, Chief Executive Officer of QSE, in the company's release. "This partnership brings together two important pieces of that equation. QSE contributes our quantum-readiness technology to help organizations measure and improve their PQC and cryptographic readiness, while Pos Digicert brings deep Malaysian market knowledge, digital trust capabilities, professional expertise and the local infrastructure needed to deliver those capabilities effectively. Together, we can provide Malaysian organizations with both the technology and local expertise required to turn post-quantum readiness from an emerging concern into measurable action."

The company framed the partnership as part of a locally delivered model for quantum readiness, and Pos Digicert's chief operating officer, Amir Suhaimi Hassan, emphasized in the release that post-quantum readiness is less about replacing a single algorithm than about understanding where cryptography exists today and managing the transition systematically without compromising trust or operational continuity. Investors following the story can track it through the Equity Insider Quantum Secure page.
In other developments across the post-quantum and cybersecurity space this week:
Palo Alto Networks, Inc. (Nasdaq: PANW)

Palo Alto Networks is one of the largest cybersecurity companies in the world, offering a broad platform spanning network security, cloud security, and security operations, and it has begun integrating post-quantum cryptography capabilities into its security products. It is referenced here to illustrate how the largest platform vendors are folding PQC into existing enterprise security stacks, a very different scale and business model from a specialized quantum-readiness company.

As one of the industry's bellwether names, Palo Alto Networks has drawn heavy investor attention around the platform-consolidation trend in cybersecurity and the addition of quantum-safe features to its offerings. It is referenced solely as sector context, a far larger and more diversified company than the featured company, and not as a peer or financial comparable.
CrowdStrike Holdings, Inc. (Nasdaq: CRWD)

CrowdStrike is a leading endpoint-security and cybersecurity-platform company whose Falcon platform is widely deployed across enterprises, and it has been positioned as a layer through which crypto-agility and PQC policy enforcement could eventually be delivered. It is included to show how endpoint and platform leaders intersect with the post-quantum migration theme.

CrowdStrike has been among the stronger-performing large-cap cybersecurity names in 2026, continuing to grow its recurring revenue base even as parts of the software sector corrected. It is referenced only as market and sector context, a substantially larger and later-stage company than the featured company, whose results are not indicative of the featured company's prospects.
International Business Machines Corporation (

IBM sits on both sides of the quantum question: it is one of the leading developers of quantum-computing hardware and, at the same time, has integrated post-quantum cryptography into its platforms and contributed to the standardization of quantum-resistant algorithms. That dual role makes it a useful reference point for the scale and maturity of the PQC transition among the largest technology companies.

IBM has publicly positioned quantum-safe technology as a major long-term theme, pairing its quantum-hardware roadmap with enterprise migration tooling. It is referenced purely as sector context, an enormously larger and more diversified company than the featured company, and its involvement is not indicative of the featured company's prospects.
SEALSQ Corp. (Nasdaq: LAES)

SEALSQ is a semiconductor and cybersecurity company focused on hardware-rooted, post-quantum-ready secure chips and PKI, positioning itself around the hardware layer of the quantum-safe transition. Of the names here, its pure focus on post-quantum security makes it a closer thematic reference to a specialized PQC company, though it operates in hardware rather than readiness assessment.

SEALSQ has drawn investor attention as one of the more direct public-market proxies for post-quantum semiconductor demand, and its shares have been notably volatile in step with quantum-computing sentiment. It is referenced only as sector context, a separate company with its own products, hardware focus, and risk profile, included to illustrate the breadth of the post-quantum opportunity rather than as a comparable.
Why the Post-Quantum Clock Reaches Beyond the Mega-Caps

The thread connecting these companies is a single regulatory and technological reality: the cryptography the digital economy runs on has a shelf life, and the migration to quantum-safe systems is now being written into government timelines and procurement decisions. The largest platform and hardware vendors are folding PQC into what they already sell. But a large share of the actual work, taking an organization from awareness to a discovered, assessed, and prioritized cryptographic environment with a credible roadmap, is a specialized discipline in its own right, and it is where focused readiness providers are positioning.

For a small, specialized company, that backdrop is opportunity and risk in equal measure. Early-stage technology companies face execution, funding, competitive, and adoption risks, and partnerships and stated intentions are not the same as realized revenue. This commentary describes a sector and the companies active within it, and is not a prediction about any company's stock or a recommendation of any kind. But with encryption deadlines now firmly on government calendars, the readiness layer of the post-quantum transition is a corner of cybersecurity worth following through the Equity Insider Quantum Secure landing page as the story develops.
